Kripa — First Teacher of the Kuru Prince: Kripa (Kripacharya) and his twin sister Kripi were born, as the Adi Parva tells it, when the seed of the sage Sharadvan Gautama fell on a clump of reeds after he saw the apsara Janapadi.
King Shantanu found the abandoned twins while hunting and raised them out of compassion (kripa), which the epic gives as the origin of the names Kripa and Kripi.
Kripa learned archery and weapon lore from his father Sharadvan and became the first instructor in arms of both the Pandava and Kaurava princes at Hastinapura.
Kripa's sister Kripi married Drona; their only son was Ashwatthama, which made Kripa Ashwatthama's maternal uncle.
Kripa remained attached to the Hastinapura court for life; he later fought on the Kaurava side at Kurukshetra and is one of the few warriors on that side who survived the war.
At the tournament (exhibition of arms), it was Kripa who challenged Karna to state his lineage before he could duel Arjuna, on the rule that princes fight only their equals in birth.
Drona — Origins, Poverty and the Feud wi: Drona was the son of the sage Bharadvaja; the epic says he was born from Bharadvaja's seed collected in a vessel (drona), which gives him his name.
As a youth Drona studied alongside Drupada, son of King Prishata of Panchala, and Drupada promised him friendship and, in some tellings, a share of his kingdom.
Drona obtained divine weapons and their lore from Rama Jamadagnya (Parashurama), who was giving away his possessions at the end of his life.
Drona lived in poverty after his marriage to Kripi; the Adi Parva tells that the boy Ashwatthama was once given flour mixed in water in place of milk, which drove Drona to seek wealth.
When Drona went to King Drupada claiming their old friendship, Drupada rejected him, saying friendship exists only between equals, and a poor brahmin could not be the friend of a king.
Humiliated by Drupada, Drona went to Hastinapura, where he lived for a time unknown in Kripa's house before Bhishma appointed him teacher of the Kuru princes.

Drona's first act at Hastinapura in the epic: the princes' ball (and, in the story, Drona's ring) had fallen into a well, and Drona retrieved it by shooting a chain of grass-blades (ishika), each piercing the one before.
Drona's teacher's fee (gurudakshina) from the princes was the capture of Drupada; the Kauravas attacked first and failed, and Arjuna with his brothers then defeated and captured Drupada.
Drona took the northern half of Panchala (capital Ahichchhatra) and returned the southern half (capital Kampilya, south of the Ganga) to Drupada, saying they were now equals and could be friends.
Drupada, nursing revenge, later performed a sacrifice through the brahmins Yaja and Upayaja to obtain a son who would kill Drona; from the sacrificial fire came Dhrishtadyumna and Draupadi.
Drona's Gurukul — Students and Specialit: Drona's students included the five Pandavas, the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra (the Kauravas), his own son Ashwatthama, princes of the Vrishni and Andhaka clans, and, according to the Critical Edition's text, Karna (called Radheya, son of the suta Adhiratha).

Popular retellings often say Drona refused to teach Karna because he was a charioteer's son; in the Critical Edition's Adi Parva Karna is listed among Drona's pupils, and his rivalry with Arjuna begins there.

The Adi Parva assigns specialities at the end of training: Arjuna excelled above all in archery and in every weapon; Bhima and Duryodhana in the mace; Nakula and Sahadeva in sword-fighting; Yudhishthira in chariot fighting; Ashwatthama in the secret lore of weapons.

Elsewhere the epic says that Bhima and Duryodhana also learned mace-fighting from Balarama, Krishna's elder brother; in the Shalya Parva Balarama calls both of them his pupils, and he is said to have favoured Duryodhana.
Drona promised Arjuna that he would make sure no archer in the world surpassed him, a promise that drives the Ekalavya episode.

The Adi Parva tells that when a gust of wind blew out the lamp while Arjuna was eating, he realised that practice could make the hand find its mark in darkness, and he began practising archery at night.

A story in the Adi Parva says Drona gave his pupils narrow-necked water pots to fill but gave Ashwatthama a wide-mouthed one so his son returned early for extra teaching; Arjuna filled his pot quickly with the Varuna weapon and so did not miss the lessons.

When a crocodile seized Drona while he bathed in the Ganga, Arjuna alone acted at once and killed it with arrows; as reward Drona gave him the Brahmashiras weapon, with the warning never to use it against ordinary human foes.
A local tradition associates Drona's teaching ground with Gurugram (Gurgaon) near Delhi; the epic itself places Drona's residence and teaching at Hastinapura.
The Bird's-Eye Test: To test his pupils' concentration, Drona set an artificial bird on a treetop as a target and asked each prince, bow drawn, what he saw.
Yudhishthira and the other princes answered that they saw the tree, the bird, Drona himself and their brothers; Drona sent each away without letting him shoot.
Arjuna answered that he saw only the bird; asked again, he said he saw only its head. Drona told him to shoot, and Arjuna severed the bird's head.

In the Critical Edition's Adi Parva the target is the bird's head (the bird is called a bhasa, a kind of bird of prey); the familiar detail that Arjuna saw only the bird's eye comes from later and popular retellings.
The episode is the epic's emblem of single-pointed concentration (ekagrata), and it is the reason the story gives for Drona's special affection for Arjuna.
Ekalavya: Ekalavya was the son of Hiranyadhanus, king of the Nishadas, a forest people; he came to Drona asking to be taught archery.

The Critical Edition says Drona refused him because he was a Nishada, and out of concern for the Kuru princes; interpretation of the refusal (caste exclusion, Drona's promise to Arjuna, royal patronage) is much debated.
Ekalavya went back to the forest, made a clay image of Drona, treated it as his teacher, and through practice became an outstanding archer.
When the princes went hunting, their dog barked at Ekalavya, and he silenced it by shooting seven arrows into its mouth at once without killing it.
Arjuna, troubled that a forest archer surpassed him, reminded Drona of his promise; Drona went to Ekalavya, who greeted him as his teacher.

Drona asked for Ekalavya's right thumb as gurudakshina, and Ekalavya cut it off and gave it without hesitation; afterwards, shooting with his fingers, he was no longer as swift as before, and Arjuna's anxiety ended.

Ekalavya reappears later as a Nishada king; in the Drona Parva Krishna names him, with Jarasandha and Shishupala, among enemies removed for the Pandavas' sake, and the Harivamsha shows him fighting the Yadavas on Jarasandha's side; accounts of his fate differ between texts.

Modern readers, writers and Dalit and Adivasi critics often read Ekalavya's thumb as a symbol of injustice by caste and birth; traditional readings stress his devotion to his teacher. Both readings are interpretations, not settled fact.
Bhima and Duryodhana — Childhood Enmity: Dhritarashtra and Gandhari had a hundred sons (the Kauravas), led by Duryodhana, and one daughter, Duhshala.

In childhood games Bhima bullied the Kauravas, pulling them under water, dragging them by the hair, and shaking trees until the boys climbing them fell; the Adi Parva gives this as a root of Duryodhana's hatred.
Duryodhana poisoned Bhima's food during a water-sport outing on the Ganga (at a place called Pramanakoti), bound the unconscious Bhima and threw him into the river.
Bhima sank to the realm of the Nagas, where snakebites counteracted the poison; the Naga Aryaka, a relative of Kunti's family, had Vasuki give him an elixir.
Bhima drank eight bowls (kundas) of the Naga elixir, which, the epic says, gave him the strength of ten thousand elephants; he returned to Hastinapura after eight days.
Number facts — Bhima and the Nagas: Bowls of elixir drunk 8 | Days before his return 8 | Elephants' strength gained 10000.
The Adi Parva says Duryodhana also tried snakes and other poisons against Bhima, and that Vidura advised the Pandavas to keep silent and stay alert rather than accuse him openly.
The Tournament and Karna's Entry: When training was complete, Drona asked Dhritarashtra to hold a public exhibition of the princes' skill (the ranga, or tournament); Vidura oversaw the arrangements, and Gandhari and Kunti watched from the stands.
The mace display between Bhima and Duryodhana turned into real rivalry, and Drona had Ashwatthama separate them before it became a fight.
Arjuna displayed mastery of divine weapons, including the fire, water, wind and cloud weapons and the weapon of invisibility (antardhana), to the crowd's acclaim.
Karna entered the arena uninvited, repeated all of Arjuna's feats, and challenged him to single combat; Duryodhana embraced him at once.
Kripa demanded that Karna declare his parents and lineage, because a prince did not have to fight an opponent of unknown birth; Karna lowered his head in shame.

Duryodhana answered that a man may be qualified for battle by birth, by valour or by leading an army, and had Karna consecrated king of Anga on the spot so that Arjuna could not refuse him as an unequal.
Asked what he wanted in return, Karna asked for Duryodhana's lifelong friendship; the bond between Karna and Duryodhana dates from this day.
When Karna's foster father, the charioteer Adhiratha, appeared, Karna bowed to him; Bhima mocked Karna as a charioteer's son who should take up the whip, not a kingdom.
Duryodhana defended Karna by arguing that the origins of heroes, like the sources of rivers, are hard to know, citing other great figures of irregular birth.
Kunti recognised Karna, her son born before her marriage (by his earrings and armour, according to the story), and fainted; Vidura revived her with sandal water, and she kept her secret.
Sunset ended the tournament before Karna and Arjuna could fight; their duel was postponed, symbolically, until the war at Kurukshetra.
Karna's Training and Curses: Before her marriage, Kunti used a mantra given to her by the sage Durvasa to invoke the sun god Surya and bore Karna; fearing disgrace, she set the baby afloat in a basket on a river, and he was found and adopted by the charioteer (suta) Adhiratha and his wife Radha.
Karna, son of Kunti by Surya and raised by Adhiratha and Radha, is called Radheya and Vasusena; he was born with armour (kavacha) and earrings (kundala), according to the epic.
The Shanti Parva (in Narada's account to Yudhishthira) says Karna went to Parashurama claiming to be a brahmin and learned the Brahmastra from him.

When an insect bored into Karna's thigh while Parashurama slept on his lap and Karna bore the pain without moving, Parashurama concluded he could not be a brahmin; he cursed Karna to forget the Brahmastra at the moment of greatest need.
Narada's account also says Karna accidentally killed a brahmin's cow, and the brahmin cursed that the earth would swallow his chariot wheel in his decisive battle.

Karna himself recalls these curses to Shalya in the Karna Parva, and both are fulfilled during his final duel with Arjuna; the order and details of the curse stories differ between the Shanti Parva, the Karna Parva and popular retellings.
Heir Apparent and Rising Jealousy: After the tournament Dhritarashtra named Yudhishthira heir apparent (yuvaraja), and the citizens openly said Yudhishthira should rule.
The Pandavas' popularity, conquests and fame deepened Duryodhana's jealousy, and he pressed Dhritarashtra to send them away from the capital.

The minister Kanika gave Dhritarashtra a famous speech of ruthless statecraft (known as Kanika's counsel), advising him to destroy rivals by craft; the Adi Parva places it just before the lac-house plot.
Dhritarashtra is shown as torn between love for his sons and duty to Pandu's sons, a tension that runs through the epic's account of the Kuru crisis.
The Lac House at Varanavata: Persuaded by Duryodhana, Dhritarashtra sent the Pandavas and Kunti to Varanavata on the pretext of a festival for Shiva (Pashupati) there.
Duryodhana's minister Purochana built them a house of highly flammable materials such as lac, resin, hemp and clay mixed with fat (the jatugriha), planning to burn them inside.

Vidura warned Yudhishthira before he left, speaking in riddles in a foreign (mleccha) tongue that only the two understood, about a fire in a dry forest from which one escapes like a creature in a burrow.
Vidura secretly sent a miner who dug an escape tunnel under the house, hidden from Purochana.
The Pandavas lived in the house for about a year, acting unsuspecting while Purochana waited for his moment.

Kunti held a feast; a Nishada woman and her five sons stayed the night drunk in the house; that night Bhima set fire to the house, beginning with Purochana's quarters, and the Pandavas and Kunti escaped through the tunnel.
Number facts — Lac house: Years lived in the house about 1 | Deaths in the fire: Nishada woman 1 | her sons 5 | Purochana 1.
Finding the bodies of the Nishada woman and her five sons, the people of Varanavata believed the Pandavas and Kunti had died; Dhritarashtra performed their funeral rites.
A boatman sent by Vidura ferried the fugitives across the Ganga, and they fled south into the forest; they later wandered as ascetics and, at Ekachakra, lived disguised as brahmins.
The deaths of the Nishada woman and her sons are an ethical problem much discussed by modern readers; the epic itself records them without comment.
Hidimba, Bakasura and the Road to Pancha: In the forest the rakshasa Hidimba sent his sister Hidimbi to kill the sleeping Pandavas; she fell in love with Bhima, who was keeping watch.

Bhima killed Hidimba in a wrestling fight, and with Kunti's and Yudhishthira's consent married Hidimbi, on condition that he would stay with her by day and return to his family at night until a son was born.
Their son Ghatotkacha grew to youth at once, as rakshasa children do in the epic, and promised to come whenever the Pandavas called him.
Vyasa visited the fugitives and directed them to the town of Ekachakra, where they lived in a brahmin's house disguised as brahmins, living on alms, with Bhima eating half of all food gathered.
The rakshasa Baka (Bakasura) near Ekachakra demanded a daily tribute of a cartload of rice, two buffaloes and the person who brought them.
Number facts — Baka's daily tribute: Cartloads of food 1 | Buffaloes 2 | Human victims 1.
When it was their host family's turn, Kunti sent Bhima in their place; Bhima ate the food himself and killed Baka, freeing the town.
On the way to Draupadi's swayamvara, Arjuna defeated the gandharva Angaraparna (also called Chitraratha) at the Ganga; the gandharva advised them to take a family priest, and they chose Dhaumya.
The gandharva Chitraratha also gave the Pandavas gandharva horses; these horses are later named among the stakes in the dice game.
Sources and Variants for the Youth Episo: These episodes are told in the Adi Parva (Book 1), mainly in the Sambhava, Jatugriha (lac house), Hidimba-vadha, Baka-vadha and Chaitraratha sub-parvas; the Critical Edition's Adi Parva has 225 chapters (adhyayas).

The Critical Edition (Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, Pune, 1919–1966) reconstructs the oldest recoverable text from many manuscripts; passages found only in some recensions are relegated to footnotes and appendices.

Details such as the bird's eye as Arjuna's target, Drona refusing Karna as a pupil, and many dialogues in television versions come from later or popular retellings rather than the Critical Edition's text.

The Pandavas' and Kauravas' childhood and education are narrated to King Janamejaya by Vaishampayana, within Ugrashravas' telling at the Naimisha forest, so every episode reaches the reader through nested narrators.

Draupadi's Birth from the Fire: Draupadi was born, along with her twin brother Dhrishtadyumna, from the fire altar of a sacrifice King Drupada had the brahmins Yaja and Upayaja perform to obtain a son who would kill Drona.
Dhrishtadyumna rose first from the fire, armoured and armed; Draupadi then emerged from the altar (vedi) as a dark-complexioned young woman of great beauty.
A voice from the sky declared that Draupadi would bring about the destruction of the Kshatriyas and serve the purpose of the gods.
Draupadi's names: Krishnaa (the dark one), Draupadi (daughter of Drupada), Panchali (princess of Panchala), Yajnaseni (born of the sacrifice) and Sairandhri (her disguise in Virata).
Shikhandi, born first as a daughter and later living as a man, was also Drupada's child and a sibling of Draupadi and Dhrishtadyumna.
Setting of the Swayamvara: Draupadi's swayamvara (self-choice ceremony) was held at Kampilya, capital of southern Panchala, Drupada's kingdom.
Drupada secretly hoped Arjuna would win Draupadi, though the Pandavas were believed to have died at Varanavata.
Kings and princes came from across the land, including Duryodhana and his brothers, Karna, Shalya, Shishupala, Jarasandha and Ashwatthama; Krishna and Balarama attended with the Yadavas.
The festivities went on for many days, and the text says Draupadi entered the arena on the sixteenth day, holding the garland for the man she would choose.
The Pandavas, disguised as brahmins, sat among the brahmins; Krishna recognised them in spite of their disguise and told Balarama.
Dhrishtadyumna announced the contest and named the assembled suitors to his sister.
The Target and the Bow: Drupada had a very stiff bow made that few could string, and set up a target that had to be hit by shooting five arrows through an opening in a device hung high in the air.
In the Critical Edition the target is a revolving or aerial device (yantra) with a hole and a mark (lakshya) beyond it; the bow had to be strung and five arrows shot through the opening.

The famous image of a revolving fish (matsya) whose eye had to be hit while aiming at its reflection in a pool of water or oil comes from later retellings, some manuscripts and regional versions; it is not in the Critical Edition's constituted text.
Many powerful kings failed even to string the bow, and some were thrown to the ground by its recoil, which the crowd met with laughter.
Number facts — Swayamvara contest: Arrows required 5 | Day Draupadi entered 16 | Successful suitors 1 (Arjuna).
Karna at the Swayamvara — Differs by Rec: Karna's part in the swayamvara is one of the best-known recension differences in the Mahabharata.

In the vulgate (the version printed with Nilakantha's commentary) and many Northern manuscripts, Karna strings the bow and is about to shoot when Draupadi declares she will not choose a charioteer's son (suta); Karna laughs bitterly, looks at the sun and puts the bow down.

In the Critical Edition's constituted text, Draupadi's public rejection of Karna is relegated to the apparatus and is not in the main text; there Karna is simply counted among the great kings who fail at the contest (manuscripts differ on the exact details of his attempt).

Popular retellings, plays and television adaptations nearly always use the rejection scene, and it underlies many modern novels that treat Karna's humiliation as a cause of his later cruelty to Draupadi in the dice hall.
Because the evidence differs, an honest account says that in some versions Draupadi rejects Karna for his birth, while in the oldest reconstructed text Karna simply fails like the other kings.
Arjuna Wins Draupadi: After the kings had failed, Arjuna rose from among the brahmins, strung the bow at once, and shot the target down with the five arrows.
The brahmins cheered and waved their deerskins; Draupadi came forward and placed her white garland on Arjuna.
The assembled Kshatriyas were enraged that a brahmin had won a Kshatriya princess and attacked Drupada; Arjuna and Bhima defended him, with Bhima using an uprooted tree as a club.
Arjuna fought Karna, and Karna withdrew, saying he would not fight on against what seemed to be the power of a brahmin; Bhima defeated Shalya in wrestling.
Krishna calmed the kings, pointing out that Draupadi had been won according to the rules of the contest.
Dhrishtadyumna secretly followed the brahmins to the potter's house where they lived and reported to Drupada that their conduct and talk of weapons showed they were Kshatriyas.
Kunti's Words and the Shared Marriage: Arriving home with Draupadi, Bhima and Arjuna announced to their mother that they had brought alms; Kunti, from inside without looking, told them to share it all together.
Seeing that the alms was Draupadi, Kunti was distressed that her words might force wrongdoing, but the rule that a mother's word must not prove false weighed on the brothers.
Yudhishthira saw that all five brothers desired Draupadi and feared that rivalry over her would split them; he decided that she would be the wife of all five.
Drupada and Dhrishtadyumna objected that one woman marrying several men was against the Vedas and customary law, and a debate on dharma followed at Drupada's court.
The marriage took place on successive days in order of seniority, Yudhishthira first; the family priest Dhaumya officiated.

The text adds that Draupadi became a maiden again after each wedding day; the claim that each brother lived with her for one year in turn is a later and popular tradition rather than a rule stated at the wedding.
Number facts — Draupadi's marriage: Husbands 5 | Wedding days 5 (one per brother, in order of age).
Justifications Offered for the Polyandry: Justification 1, Kunti's word: Kunti's instruction to share must not be made false, which the brothers treat as binding.

Justification 2, precedent: Yudhishthira cites old precedents of polyandry, such as Jatila of the Gautama lineage, said to have married seven sages, and Varkshi, a sage's daughter said to have married ten brothers, the Prachetas.

Justification 3, Draupadi's previous birth: Vyasa tells Drupada that in an earlier life Draupadi, a sage's daughter, asked Shiva for a husband five times, and Shiva granted her five husbands in her next birth; later tradition names this earlier woman Nalayani.

Justification 4, the five Indras: Vyasa tells a story in which five former Indras were reborn as the Pandavas and the goddess Shri (Lakshmi) was born as Draupadi to be their common wife; Vyasa gives Drupada divine sight to see their divine forms.
Justification 5, family unity: the story itself makes it clear that the arrangement keeps the five brothers from fighting over Draupadi.

Many scholars read the episode as a narrative effort to explain an unusual polyandrous marriage; whether it reflects an older custom is debated, and the epic itself presents the marriage as needing exceptional justification.
Narada's Rule and its Consequences: To prevent quarrels over Draupadi, the sage Narada told the brothers the story of the asura brothers Sunda and Upasunda, who killed each other over the apsara Tilottama.
The brothers agreed that if one of them intruded while another was alone with Draupadi, the intruder would go into exile as a celibate (brahmacharin) for twelve years.

Arjuna broke the rule to fetch his weapons from the room where Yudhishthira was with Draupadi so he could help a brahmin whose cattle had been stolen; he insisted on going into exile even though Yudhishthira forgave him.

The rule specified twelve years of exile, but the epic's account of Arjuna's journey is chronologically loose, and readers have noted that his marriages during the 'celibate' exile sit uneasily with the vow.
Number facts — Narada's rule: Exile for intrusion 12 years.
Draupadi's Sons and the Pandavas' Other: Draupadi bore each Pandava one son, together called the Upapandavas: Prativindhya (by Yudhishthira), Sutasoma (by Bhima), Shrutakarman (by Arjuna), Shatanika (by Nakula) and Shrutasena (by Sahadeva).
All five sons of Draupadi were killed by Ashwatthama in the night raid on the Pandava camp after the war.

The Adi Parva also lists the Pandavas' other wives and sons: Yudhishthira and Devika (son Yaudheya); Bhima and Hidimbi (son Ghatotkacha) and Bhima and Balandhara (son Sarvaga); Nakula and Karenumati (son Niramitra); Sahadeva and Vijaya (son Suhotra).
Arjuna married Ulupi (son Iravat), Chitrangada of Manipura (son Babhruvahana) and Subhadra, Krishna's sister (son Abhimanyu), during and after his exile.
Number facts — sons of Draupadi: Prativindhya 1 | Sutasoma 1 | Shrutakarman 1 | Shatanika 1 | Shrutasena 1 (total 5).
Return to Hastinapura and the Half-Kingd: News that the Pandavas were alive and allied to Panchala by marriage reached Hastinapura, where Duryodhana and Karna debated how to respond.
Duryodhana proposed covert schemes, such as sowing discord between the brothers or turning Draupadi against them; Karna argued instead for an immediate open attack before the Pandavas grew stronger.
Bhishma and Drona advised Dhritarashtra to welcome the Pandavas back and give them half the kingdom, and Vidura was sent to bring them, with Kunti and Draupadi, to Hastinapura.
Dhritarashtra gave Yudhishthira the region of Khandavaprastha, a forested and undeveloped half of the realm, where the Pandavas built Indraprastha.
These events form the Vaivahika (wedding), Viduragamana (Vidura's coming) and Rajyalabha (gaining the kingdom) sub-parvas of the Adi Parva.

Founding of Indraprastha: Dhritarashtra gave the Pandavas Khandavaprastha, and with Krishna's help they built a city there named Indraprastha, described in the epic as rich, walled and moated, with broad streets and splendid buildings.
Some retellings say the divine architect Vishvakarma built Indraprastha at Indra's command; the Critical Edition describes the city's building more generally.
Indraprastha is traditionally identified with the area of present-day Delhi, often with the site of the Purana Qila; the epic itself gives no map coordinates.
Yudhishthira ruled Indraprastha justly, and the epic describes the kingdom as prosperous and well-governed under him.
Arjuna's Exile, Pilgrimage and Marriages: Under Narada's rule Arjuna left Indraprastha on a twelve-year exile and pilgrimage after intruding on Yudhishthira and Draupadi to fetch his weapons for a brahmin.
At the Ganga, Ulupi, a Naga princess, drew Arjuna to the Naga realm and married him; their son was Iravat (Iravan).
At Manipura Arjuna married Chitrangada, the king's only daughter, on condition that her son would stay to continue her father's line; their son was Babhruvahana.
In the far south Arjuna freed five apsaras who had been cursed to live as crocodiles in sacred bathing places.
At Prabhasa and Dvaraka, with Krishna's encouragement, Arjuna carried off Subhadra, Krishna's sister; Balarama was angry at first but was reconciled, and the marriage was celebrated.
Subhadra's son by Arjuna was Abhimanyu, later married to Uttara, princess of Virata, and father of Parikshit.
Draupadi was hurt at first by Arjuna's marriage to Subhadra; Subhadra came to her dressed as a cowherd woman and won her acceptance.
These events are told in the Arjuna-vanavasa, Subhadra-harana and Harana-harika sub-parvas of the Adi Parva.
Burning of the Khandava Forest: Agni, the fire god, had become sick from consuming too much ghee offered in King Shvetaki's sacrifices, and was told by Brahma that eating the creatures and plants of the Khandava forest would cure him.

The vulgate expands the Shvetaki story at length (including a twelve-year rite and the sage Durvasa serving as priest); much of this elaboration is not in the Critical Edition's main text, so its details should be treated as variant material.
Agni had tried seven times to burn Khandava, but Indra protected it because his friend the Naga Takshaka lived there, and put out the fires with rain.
Agni came to Krishna and Arjuna, picnicking on the bank of the Yamuna, disguised as a brahmin, and asked them to help him burn the forest.

To equip them, Varuna gave Arjuna the Gandiva bow, two inexhaustible quivers and a chariot with white horses and a monkey banner (kapidhvaja); Krishna received the Sudarshana discus and the mace Kaumodaki.

Krishna and Arjuna circled the forest in their chariots and shot down creatures that tried to escape, while fighting off Indra and the gods; Indra finally withdrew, and a heavenly voice told him Takshaka was away at Kurukshetra.
The epic says the fire burned for fifteen days, and that only six beings escaped: Takshaka's son Ashvasena, the asura Maya, and four Sharngaka birds, sons of the sage Mandapala and the bird Jarita.
Number facts — Khandava: Agni's failed attempts before 7 | Days the fire burned 15 | Survivors named 6 (Ashvasena 1, Maya 1, Sharngaka birds 4).
Indra was pleased with Arjuna and promised him divine weapons once Arjuna had pleased Shiva; Krishna asked for eternal friendship with Arjuna.

Takshaka's son Ashvasena, whose mother died in the fire, bears a lasting grudge: in the Karna Parva he enters Karna's arrow to strike Arjuna, and Krishna saves Arjuna by pressing the chariot down so the arrow only knocks off his diadem.

In the frame story Takshaka later kills Arjuna's grandson Parikshit, but the epic gives a sage's curse (by Shringin, son of Shamika) as the cause, not the Khandava fire; linking the two as revenge is an interpretation.

Modern readers often see the Khandava burning as ethically troubling, and some scholars read it as a mythic memory of clearing forest land for settlement; these are interpretations, not statements of the text.
Maya and the Maya Sabha: The asura architect Maya, spared by Arjuna during the Khandava fire, offered to build something in gratitude, and at Krishna's suggestion built an assembly hall (sabha) for Yudhishthira.
Maya brought materials from the lake Bindusaras near Mount Kailasa, including a great mace that he gave to Bhima and the conch Devadatta that he gave to Arjuna.
The epic says the hall took fourteen months to build, measured ten thousand cubits (kishkus) around, and was carried and guarded by eight thousand rakshasas called Kinkaras.
Number facts — Maya Sabha: Months to build 14 | Size around 10000 cubits | Rakshasa guards 8000.
The hall was famous for its illusions: crystal floors that looked like water, pools that looked like solid floor, and walls that looked like doors.
The Maya Sabha's illusions are the setting of Duryodhana's humiliation, which led directly to the dice game.
Narada's Visit and the Idea of the Rajas: The sage Narada visited Yudhishthira in the new hall and asked him a long series of questions about how he governed (the 'kaccid' questions, beginning 'I hope that…'), a short treatise on kingship.
Narada described the halls of the gods Indra, Yama, Varuna, Kubera and Brahma, and said that King Harishchandra had a place in Indra's hall because he had performed the Rajasuya.
Narada brought a message that Pandu, in Yama's hall, wished Yudhishthira to perform the Rajasuya, the royal consecration sacrifice that proclaims a king as emperor (samrat).
Yudhishthira consulted his brothers and Krishna; Krishna said the Rajasuya was impossible while Jarasandha of Magadha held power over so many kings.
Jarasandha of Magadha: Jarasandha was king of Magadha, with his capital at Girivraja (traditionally identified with Rajgir in Bihar).

The epic says Jarasandha was born in two halves to the two queens of King Brihadratha after they shared a mango blessed by the sage Chandakaushika, and was joined together by the rakshasi Jara, which gives him his name.
Jarasandha had imprisoned eighty-six kings and meant to sacrifice them to Rudra (Shiva) once he had a hundred, needing only fourteen more.
Number facts — Jarasandha's captives: Kings imprisoned 86 | Target 100 | Still needed 14.

Jarasandha's enmity toward Krishna stemmed from Krishna's killing of Kamsa, who was married to Jarasandha's daughters; Krishna told Yudhishthira that the Yadavas had left Mathura and moved west to Dvaraka because of Jarasandha's attacks; Puranic texts such as the Bhagavata count seventeen or eighteen attacks, but numbers differ between texts.
Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna entered Girivraja disguised as snataka brahmins, avoiding the gate, and challenged Jarasandha to single combat.
Jarasandha chose to wrestle Bhima; the text says they began on the first day of the month of Karttika and fought day and night without rest until Jarasandha tired on the fourteenth night.
Number facts — Bhima vs Jarasandha: Days of continuous wrestling 13 | Night Jarasandha tired 14.

Bhima lifted Jarasandha, whirled him around and broke him in two; the popular detail that Krishna showed Bhima how by splitting a blade of grass and throwing the halves in opposite directions comes from later retellings, not the Critical Edition.
The imprisoned kings were freed, Jarasandha's son Sahadeva was installed on the Magadha throne, and the freed kings promised to support Yudhishthira's Rajasuya.
Conquest of the Four Directions: Before the Rajasuya, the four younger Pandavas led campaigns of conquest (digvijaya) to gather tribute: Arjuna to the north, Bhima to the east, Sahadeva to the south and Nakula to the west.

Arjuna's northern campaign went into the Himalayan regions and, in the epic's account, reached the border of the land of the Uttara Kurus, whose guardians told him it could not be conquered by men; he accepted tribute and turned back.

On his southern campaign Sahadeva sent envoys to Vibhishana of Lanka, who accepted Yudhishthira's overlordship and sent tribute; the detail that Ghatotkacha was the envoy belongs to Southern-recension manuscripts and later retellings rather than the Critical Edition's main text.
Number facts — Digvijaya by direction: North Arjuna | East Bhima | South Sahadeva | West Nakula.
The campaigns are told in the Digvijaya sub-parva of the Sabha Parva (Book 2).
The Rajasuya Sacrifice: Yudhishthira performed the Rajasuya at Indraprastha, attended by kings from every region, the Kuru elders, and the Kauravas.
The Sabha Parva names the main priests: Vyasa as the Brahman priest, Susaman as Udgatar (chanter of Saman verses), Yajnavalkya as Adhvaryu, and Paila and Dhaumya as Hotars.

Duties were shared among kin: Duryodhana received the tribute and gifts, Dushasana supervised food, Ashwatthama attended the brahmins, Kripa looked after gold and jewels, Vidura managed the expenses, and Krishna is said to have washed the feet of the brahmins.

Duryodhana later told his father in detail about the vast tribute he had received at the Rajasuya, including horses, gems, cloth, and the 'ant gold' brought by northern peoples; his envy of this wealth fed the dice plot.
The Rajasuya made Yudhishthira emperor (samrat), a rank Duryodhana could not tolerate.

Vyasa warned Yudhishthira after the sacrifice that in thirteen years a great destruction of the Kshatriyas would come about with Yudhishthira as its cause; Yudhishthira vowed to speak no harsh word to anyone, to avoid conflict.
Number facts — Vyasa's prophecy: Years until the destruction 13.
Shishupala and the First Honour: At the Rajasuya, the first honour (agrapuja, the arghya offering) had to go to the most worthy guest; Bhishma proposed Krishna, and Sahadeva made the offering.
Shishupala, king of Chedi and Krishna's cousin, objected, insulting Krishna as no king and a cowherd, and insulting Bhishma and the Pandavas for honouring him.
Shishupala had been the betrothed suitor of Rukmini, whom Krishna carried off and married, which the epic treats as part of his hostility.

Bhishma told the assembly that Shishupala had been born with three eyes and four arms, and that a voice had said the extra limbs would fall away in the lap of the man who would kill him; they fell away in Krishna's lap.
Shishupala's mother, Krishna's paternal aunt (a sister of Vasudeva), begged mercy, and Krishna promised to pardon a hundred offences by her son.
Krishna listed earlier crimes of Shishupala, such as attacking Dvaraka while Krishna was away and disrupting his father's horse sacrifice.
When Shishupala went beyond the hundredth offence, Krishna cut off his head with the Sudarshana discus; a radiance rose from Shishupala's body and entered Krishna.
Number facts — Krishna's promise: Offences to be pardoned 100.
After Shishupala's death, his son Dhrishtaketu was installed as king of Chedi, and the Rajasuya was completed.
Duryodhana's Humiliation in the Maya Sab: Duryodhana stayed on at Indraprastha after the Rajasuya and wandered through the Maya Sabha, where the hall's illusions tricked him again and again.

He mistook a crystal floor for a pool and lifted his garments; then he walked into a real pool he thought was solid floor and fell in, soaking his clothes; he also tried to walk through a wall that looked like a door.
In the Sabha Parva narrative, Bhima laughed at him, along with servants, and Yudhishthira had dry clothes brought.

When Duryodhana later complains to his father, the circle of mockers widens (in some passages to the other Pandavas and to Draupadi with her women); exactly who laughed varies between passages and manuscripts, and popular retellings make Draupadi the chief mocker.

The famous line in which Draupadi says 'the son of a blind man is blind' is a later and popular addition, made familiar by plays and television; it is not in the Critical Edition's Sanskrit text, and Draupadi's taunt should not be cited as part of the oldest epic.
Duryodhana returned to Hastinapura burning with envy and shame, told Shakuni he would rather die than see the Pandavas' wealth, and Shakuni proposed winning their kingdom through dice.
Sources and Variants for the Indraprasth: Khandava and the founding of Indraprastha are told at the end of the Adi Parva; the Maya Sabha, Narada's visit, Jarasandha, the digvijaya, the Rajasuya and Shishupala's death are told in the Sabha Parva (Book 2).

The Critical Edition's Sabha Parva has 72 chapters (adhyayas), and includes the sub-parvas Sabhakriya, Lokapala-sabhakhyana, Rajasuyarambha, Jarasandha-vadha, Digvijaya, Rajasuyika, Arghabhiharana, Shishupala-vadha, Dyuta and Anudyuta.
Number facts — Critical Edition adhyaya counts: Adi Parva 225 | Sabha Parva 72.

Popular retellings often merge or compress these episodes, for example placing Duryodhana's fall in the Maya Sabha at the Rajasuya itself and adding Draupadi's 'blind man's son' taunt; the Critical Edition keeps the humiliation as a separate scene after the sacrifice and lacks that taunt.

Shakuni's Plan and the Invitation: Shakuni, prince of Gandhara and brother of Gandhari, proposed that Duryodhana win the Pandavas' wealth by a game of dice, since Yudhishthira loved dice but played poorly, while Shakuni was a master.
Dhritarashtra hesitated and consulted Vidura, who warned that the game would destroy the family; Dhritarashtra let himself be persuaded by Duryodhana anyway.
Dhritarashtra had a new assembly hall built for the game, described as crystal-arched and splendid, and sent Vidura to invite Yudhishthira.
Yudhishthira accepted, saying he would not refuse a challenge or disobey his elder Dhritarashtra's summons, and adding that all was ruled by fate.
In the Vana Parva Krishna says he was away fighting King Shalva of Saubha at the time and would have stopped the dice game had he been present.
Rules and Fairness of the Game: Duryodhana staked the wealth on the Kaurava side while Shakuni threw the dice for him; Yudhishthira objected that playing through a proxy was improper, but he went on playing.
Yudhishthira accused Shakuni of cheating at the outset; Shakuni replied that a skilled player defeats an unskilled one and anyone afraid should not play.

The Sabha Parva presents Shakuni as winning by deceitful skill (nikriti); the folk story that Shakuni's dice were made from his father's bones and obeyed him is a much later regional tradition, not part of the Sanskrit epic.
Each round was settled by one throw, and Shakuni won every round, announcing each victory with the word 'won' (jitam).
Dice Game Stakes in Sequence: Stakes in order, as given in the Sabha Parva (summaries vary slightly): 1 a precious pearl or jewel set in gold; 2 jars of gold coins; 3 Yudhishthira's royal chariot; 4 serving women; 5 serving men; 6 elephants; 7 chariots; 8 the gandharva horses; 9 carts and wagons; 10 soldiers; 11 chests of gold; 12 cattle, horses, sheep and goats; 13 the city, the land, and all wealth except that of brahmins; 14 the princes' ornaments; 15 Nakula; 16 Sahadeva; 17 Arjuna; 18 Bhima; 19 Yudhishthira himself; 20 Draupadi.

Dice stake sequence (round number by category): Jewel 1 | Gold 2 | Royal chariot 3 | Serving women 4 | Serving men 5 | Elephants 6 | Chariots 7 | Gandharva horses 8 | Carts 9 | Soldiers 10 | Treasure chests 11 | Livestock 12 | Kingdom and wealth 13 | Ornaments 14 | Nakula 15 | Sahadeva 16 | Arjuna 17 | Bhima 18 | Yudhishthira 19 | Draupadi 20.

Quantities for some stakes as given in common translations (counts differ between manuscripts and translations): Jars of gold 100 (each with 1000 gold pieces) | Horses drawing the royal chariot 8 | Serving women 100000 | Serving men 100000 | Elephants 1000 | Chariots 1000 | Carts and wagons 10000 | Soldiers 60000 | Treasure chests 400.
Stake categories (count of rounds): Material wealth 14 | Brothers 4 | Yudhishthira himself 1 | Draupadi 1.
Vidura broke in partway through the material stakes, warning Dhritarashtra that Duryodhana would destroy the Kurus and urging him to stop; the game went on.
After his wealth was gone, Yudhishthira staked Nakula, then Sahadeva; Shakuni taunted him for staking Madri's sons first but holding back Bhima and Arjuna, and Yudhishthira staked Arjuna and Bhima.
Having lost his brothers, Yudhishthira staked himself and lost; Shakuni said it was wrong to lose oneself while one still had something to stake, and named Draupadi.
Yudhishthira praised Draupadi's qualities and staked her; when Shakuni won, the elders in the hall were dismayed, Vidura held his head in his hands, and Duryodhana's party rejoiced.
Number facts — total rounds in the first game, as commonly counted: Rounds lost by Yudhishthira 20 | Rounds won 0.
Draupadi's Question: Duryodhana sent the usher (pratikamin) to fetch Draupadi as a won slave; Draupadi sent him back to ask Yudhishthira, before the assembly, whom he had lost first, himself or her.
The force of Draupadi's question: if Yudhishthira had already lost himself and become a slave, could he still own, and therefore stake, his wife?
Yudhishthira remained silent and gave no answer; Duryodhana told Draupadi to come and ask the question herself.
Dushasana went to the women's quarters and dragged Draupadi into the hall by her hair, even though she said she was in her monthly period and wearing a single garment.
In the hall Draupadi appealed to the elders and asked the assembly to decide whether she had been won by right; her question is never clearly answered in the epic.

Bhishma said that dharma was subtle and he could not settle the question: a man who no longer owns himself cannot stake what belongs to another, yet a wife is subject to her husband, and Yudhishthira himself had admitted his loss.
Drona, Kripa and most of the kings in the hall kept silent, a silence that later tradition and modern readers often condemn.

Vidura told the assembly it had a duty to answer, illustrating with the story of Prahlada, who judged truthfully between his own son Virochana and the brahmin Sudhanvan even though truth went against his son.
Vikarna's Objection: Vikarna, one of Dhritarashtra's sons, was the only Kaurava to speak up for Draupadi in the hall.

Vikarna argued that Draupadi had not been fairly won: Yudhishthira was under the spell of dice, one of the recognised vices of kings (with hunting, drinking and women); he staked her after losing himself; she was the common wife of all five brothers; and Shakuni, not Yudhishthira, had proposed her as a stake.
The assembly applauded Vikarna, but Karna rebuked him as a boy speaking out of turn and claimed Draupadi had been won because Yudhishthira had staked everything he owned.
Vikarna fought on the Kaurava side at Kurukshetra despite his objection, and was killed by Bhima, who mourned him; his position is often cited as an example of conscience without power.
Karna, Duryodhana and Dushasana in the H: Karna declared that a woman with five husbands was a bandhaki (an unchaste woman), so there was nothing wrong in bringing her into the hall in one garment or even stripping her, and he ordered the Pandavas and Draupadi to be stripped of their garments.
The Pandavas took off their upper garments and sat silent; Dushasana then began pulling off Draupadi's garment.
Duryodhana bared his left thigh to Draupadi, mocking and inviting her to sit on it; Bhima vowed to break that thigh in battle, and later did so in their mace duel.
Duryodhana and Karna called Draupadi a slave (dasi) and told her to go to the servants' quarters or choose another husband who would not gamble her away.

Karna's cruelty to Draupadi in the hall is often explained in later retellings as revenge for her rejection of him at the swayamvara, a scene found in some recensions but not in the Critical Edition's main text.
The Disrobing and the Miracle — Variant: As Dushasana pulled at Draupadi's garment, another garment of the same kind appeared in its place again and again, in many colours, until a heap of cloth lay in the hall and Dushasana gave up exhausted.
In the vulgate (Nilakantha) and many manuscripts, Draupadi prays to Krishna (calling him Govinda and dweller in Dvaraka), and the endless cloth is understood as Krishna's protection.

In the Critical Edition's constituted text, the explicit prayer to Krishna is not included in the main text; the garments simply keep appearing, with no named divine agent, and the miracle is usually read as the power of dharma or Draupadi's own virtue.
Some scholars have questioned how much of even the multiplying-garment scene belongs to the oldest text, because the passage is short and varies greatly among manuscripts; this remains debated.

Later devotional traditions (for example in Bhagavata-influenced and regional bhakti retellings) make Draupadi's surrender to Krishna the centre of the scene; the story that Krishna repaid Draupadi for once binding his cut finger with her sari is a popular later legend, not in the Sanskrit epic.
Television and popular art often show Krishna in person sending the sari; this is a modern visual convention, not a scene of the epic, where Krishna is absent from Hastinapura.
Because the explanations differ, an accurate summary is: the garment miraculously did not run out, and versions attribute this to dharma, to Draupadi's virtue, or to Krishna's grace.
The Vows Made in the Hall: Bhima vowed to tear open Dushasana's chest and drink his blood in battle, a vow fulfilled during the Kurukshetra war in the Karna Parva.
Bhima vowed to break Duryodhana's thigh with his mace, fulfilled in the final mace duel at the end of the war.
Before leaving for exile, Arjuna vowed to kill Karna, Sahadeva vowed to kill Shakuni, and Nakula vowed to destroy those who had insulted Draupadi.

In the epic Draupadi keeps her hair unbound as a sign of the insult, and in the Udyoga Parva she holds up her loosened hair before Krishna as she demands war; the popular idea that she vowed to wash her hair in Dushasana's blood comes from later works such as the Sanskrit play Venisamhara and regional retellings.
Draupadi's Boons and the Release: Ill omens erupted in the hall: jackals howled in the fire-sanctuary and donkeys brayed; Gandhari and Vidura urged Dhritarashtra to act.
Dhritarashtra offered Draupadi a boon; she chose the freedom of Yudhishthira, so that her son Prativindhya would not be called a slave's son.
With a second boon she asked for the freedom of Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula and Sahadeva, with their weapons and chariots.
Offered a third boon, Draupadi declined, saying that a Kshatriya woman may ask only two, while a Vaishya may ask one, a Kshatriya man three and a brahmin a hundred.
Number facts — boons Draupadi cites as proper: Vaishya 1 | Kshatriya woman 2 | Kshatriya man 3 | Brahmin 100.
Karna remarked that Draupadi had been like a boat that carried the drowning Pandavas to shore.
Dhritarashtra returned all the Pandavas' lost wealth and kingdom and sent them home to Indraprastha with his blessing.
The Second Dice Game (Anudyuta): Duryodhana, with Dushasana, Karna and Shakuni, persuaded Dhritarashtra to recall Yudhishthira for one more game, arguing that the Pandavas would now take revenge.
Gandhari urged Dhritarashtra to abandon Duryodhana for the sake of the family, but he did not; Yudhishthira, already on his way home, turned back.

The stake of the second game was a single throw: the losers would spend twelve years in the forest and a thirteenth year incognito, and if discovered during the thirteenth year they would go into exile for another twelve years.
Shakuni won the single throw, and the Pandavas, with Draupadi, prepared to leave for the forest dressed in deerskins.
Number facts — second game: Throws 1 | Forest exile 12 years | Incognito 1 year | Penalty if discovered 12 more years of forest exile (and another incognito year).
Departure for Exile: Vidura described to Dhritarashtra how the Pandavas left: Yudhishthira with his face covered so his angry gaze would not burn the people, Bhima showing his mighty arms, Arjuna scattering sand like arrows, Sahadeva with his face smeared, Nakula covered in dust, and Draupadi weeping with her hair loose.
The priest Dhaumya walked ahead chanting Saman hymns associated with death, as a sign of what would befall the Kurus in battle.

Kunti, too old and delicate for the forest, stayed in Vidura's house; later, when Krishna and Dhrishtadyumna visited the exiles in the Kamyaka forest, Krishna took Subhadra and Abhimanyu to Dvaraka and Dhrishtadyumna took Draupadi's sons to Panchala.
Drona said publicly that the Pandavas would return in the fourteenth year and destroy the Kauravas, and that he would fight for Duryodhana nevertheless.
Interpretations and Debates about the Di: Draupadi's question has been discussed for centuries as a problem in dharma: whether a man who has lost his own freedom can stake another, and whether a wife is property.
Yudhishthira's gambling is presented by the epic as both a personal weakness and a duty (a king does not refuse a challenge), and later tradition debates how far he is to blame.
The silence of Bhishma, Drona and Kripa is often read as a failure of the elders, and the epic itself returns to it in later books.
Some scholars connect the dice game with the dicing ritual of the Vedic Rajasuya, suggesting the scene echoes royal consecration rites; this is a scholarly hypothesis.
The dice game is told in the Dyuta and Anudyuta sub-parvas at the end of the Sabha Parva (Book 2).

Terms of the Exile: Under the terms of the second dice game, the Pandavas had to live twelve years in the forest and then one year incognito (ajnatavasa), unrecognised by anyone.
If they were discovered during the thirteenth year, they had to begin the cycle again with another twelve years in the forest.
Exile timeline (years): Forest exile 12 | Incognito year 1 | Total 13.
Exile penalty if discovered (years): Additional forest exile 12 | Additional incognito 1.
Draupadi went into exile with her husbands; the family priest Dhaumya and many brahmins followed them at first.
Exile Timeline and Main Episodes: Year 1 of exile: the Pandavas leave Hastinapura, receive the inexhaustible food vessel from Surya, kill Kirmira at the entrance to the Kamyaka forest, and are visited by Krishna.

Around the early years: the Pandavas live in the Dvaita forest by the Dvaita lake; Draupadi, Bhima and Yudhishthira debate patience and action; Arjuna leaves for the Himalaya to obtain divine weapons.
Arjuna spends five years in Indra's heaven learning weapons, music and dance before rejoining his brothers on Mount Gandhamadana.
Middle years: Yudhishthira hears the Nala story, the brothers make a long pilgrimage to sacred places with the sage Lomasha, Bhima meets Hanuman, and Jatasura is killed.

Later years, in the Vana Parva's order: Markandeya's long discourses, the Draupadi-Satyabhama dialogue, the Ghosha-yatra (cattle-inspection expedition) of Duryodhana, Draupadi's abduction by Jayadratha (after which Markandeya tells the Rama and Savitri stories), and Indra's taking of Karna's armour.
End of the twelfth year: at the Dvaita forest the Yaksha questions Yudhishthira at the lake and grants the boon that the Pandavas will not be recognised in their thirteenth year.
Exile timeline (years, firmly stated in the text): Forest years 12 | Arjuna in Indra's heaven 5 | Incognito year in Virata 1.
The epic does not assign a precise year to every forest episode, and its internal chronology is loose; the ordering above follows the sequence of the Vana Parva.
Kamyaka and Dvaita Forests: The Kamyaka forest, described as lying near the Sarasvati river at the edge of the desert, was one of the Pandavas' two main forest homes during exile.
The Dvaita forest, around the Dvaita lake, was their other main home; they moved between the two forests during the exile.

In the Mrigasvapnodbhava sub-parva, the surviving deer of the Dvaita forest appeared to Yudhishthira in a dream and begged the Pandavas to move on because their hunting had thinned the herds; the Pandavas returned to the Kamyaka forest.

Yudhishthira prayed to the sun god Surya on Dhaumya's advice, reciting Surya's hundred and eight names, and received a copper vessel (the akshaya patra) that supplied unlimited food each day until Draupadi had eaten.
Number facts — Surya's gift: Names of Surya recited 108 | Food vessel 1 (inexhaustible until Draupadi had eaten each day).
Krishna visited them in the Kamyaka forest with Yadava heroes; Draupadi poured out her grief and anger, and Krishna promised that her humiliation would be avenged and she would be a queen again.
Krishna explained his absence from the dice game by his war with Shalva of Saubha, who had attacked Dvaraka.
Draupadi and Satyabhama, Krishna's wife, had a conversation in which Draupadi described how she served her husbands and managed the household at Indraprastha (the Draupadi-Satyabhama dialogue).
Kirmira, Jatasura and Other Rakshasas: Kirmira, a rakshasa who was the brother of Baka and a friend of Hidimba, blocked the Pandavas' way into the Kamyaka forest at night, intending revenge; Bhima killed him.
Vidura told Dhritarashtra the story of Kirmira's death, after the sage Maitreya had cursed Duryodhana for ignoring his advice, saying Bhima would break his thigh in battle.
Jatasura, a rakshasa disguised as a brahmin, carried off Yudhishthira, Nakula, Sahadeva and Draupadi while Bhima was away; Bhima pursued him and killed him.
On Mount Gandhamadana, Bhima killed yakshas and rakshasas guarding Kubera's lotus lake, including the yaksha Maniman, while fetching flowers for Draupadi; Kubera later made peace with the Pandavas.
Debates on Patience and Action: In the Dvaita forest Draupadi challenged Yudhishthira's patience, contrasting his calm with her suffering and arguing that forgiveness must have limits.
Draupadi told the old story of Prahlada and Bali on when forgiveness and when anger is proper, and she questioned how a just god could allow such suffering.
Bhima urged Yudhishthira to break the terms and win back the kingdom at once, arguing that thirteen months might stand in for thirteen years, as the Veda permits substitutes in ritual.
Yudhishthira refused to break his promise, saying truth and keeping his word mattered more than the kingdom, and that they would wait out the agreed time.
These dialogues are among the epic's most important discussions of fate (daiva), human effort (purusha-kara), anger and forgiveness.
Arjuna's Kirata Episode and the Pashupat: Vyasa taught Yudhishthira a secret knowledge (pratismriti) to pass on to Arjuna, and Arjuna went to Indrakila in the Himalaya to do austerities to win divine weapons.

Shiva came to test Arjuna disguised as a Kirata (mountain hunter), with the goddess Uma; a demon in the form of a boar (named Muka) charged at Arjuna, and Arjuna and the Kirata shot it at the same moment.

Arjuna and the Kirata quarrelled over who had killed the boar; in the fight, Arjuna's arrows failed, his inexhaustible quivers ran empty, and the Kirata took his bow; they wrestled and Arjuna fell unconscious.

Arjuna realised his opponent was Shiva and worshipped him; pleased with his courage, Shiva gave him the Pashupata weapon, warning him never to use it against weaker opponents because it could destroy the world.
The guardians of the directions then gave Arjuna their weapons: Yama his staff, Varuna his noose, and Kubera his weapon of invisibility (antardhana); Indra invited him to heaven.
The episode inspired the Sanskrit court epic Kiratarjuniya by Bharavi (about the 6th century CE), one of the classical great poems (mahakavya).
The episode is told in the Kairata (Kirata) sub-parva of the Vana Parva.
Arjuna's Sojourn in Indra's Heaven: Indra's charioteer Matali carried Arjuna to Amaravati, Indra's city, where Arjuna stayed five years learning the use of divine weapons.
The gandharva Chitrasena taught Arjuna music and dance in heaven, skills he later used as Brihannala in Virata.
The apsara Urvashi approached Arjuna; he refused her because, as wife of his ancestor Pururavas, he regarded her as a mother of his line. She cursed him to live as a eunuch, dancing among women.
Indra limited Urvashi's curse to one year at a time of Arjuna's choosing, and Arjuna used it for his incognito year in Virata.
As his teacher's fee to Indra, Arjuna defeated the Nivatakavachas, demons living under the sea, and destroyed the flying city Hiranyapura of the Paulomas and Kalakeyas.
Number facts — Arjuna in heaven: Years in Amaravati 5 | Duration of Urvashi's curse as limited by Indra 1 year.
Lomasha, a sage sent by Indra, came to the Pandavas on earth with news of Arjuna and accompanied them on their pilgrimage.
Pilgrimage, Hanuman and Stories Heard in: The sage Brihadashva told Yudhishthira the story of Nala and Damayanti (Nalopakhyana), about a king who also lost his kingdom at dice, and taught Yudhishthira the secret of dice (akshahridaya).

Guided by Lomasha, the Pandavas visited many tirthas (sacred places) and heard stories of Agastya, Rishyashringa, Bhagiratha bringing down the Ganga, Parashurama, Chyavana, Mandhata, and King Shibi saving a dove from a hawk.

Fetching the fragrant saugandhika lotus for Draupadi on Mount Gandhamadana, Bhima met an old monkey blocking the path who turned out to be Hanuman, his elder brother as fellow son of the wind god Vayu; Bhima could not lift his tail.
Hanuman showed Bhima his giant form and promised to sit on Arjuna's banner and roar with Bhima in battle.
A great serpent seized Bhima in the forest; it was King Nahusha, cursed long ago, and Yudhishthira freed both by answering his questions on what makes a true brahmin.

The sage Markandeya told many stories, including the fish and the great flood (the Matsya story), the story of Rama (Ramopakhyana), Savitri and Satyavan, and the righteous hunter (dharmavyadha) who taught a proud brahmin.
The Ghosha-yatra and Duryodhana's Shame: Duryodhana, Karna and Shakuni went to the Dvaita forest with a great retinue on the pretext of inspecting their cattle herds, intending to flaunt their wealth before the exiled Pandavas.
The gandharva Chitrasena and his followers fought the Kauravas, routed Karna and captured Duryodhana and his family.
Yudhishthira sent Bhima and Arjuna to rescue Duryodhana, saying family quarrels do not allow outsiders to humiliate the family; Arjuna persuaded Chitrasena to free him.
Ashamed at being saved by his enemies, Duryodhana resolved to fast to death; demons (danavas) from the underworld and Karna's promises persuaded him to give up the fast.
Karna then made a conquest of the four directions for Duryodhana, and Duryodhana performed a great Vaishnava sacrifice, since a Rajasuya could not be performed while Yudhishthira lived.
Karna vowed not to wash his feet until he had killed Arjuna.
The Durvasa Episode — Recension Note: In the vulgate, Duryodhana sends the irascible sage Durvasa with a large company of disciples to the Pandavas after Draupadi has already eaten, so the food vessel is empty and the sage's curse seems certain.
In that version Draupadi prays to Krishna, who eats a single leaf of vegetable stuck to the vessel; the sages, bathing in the river, suddenly feel full and slip away.
This Durvasa episode is found in the vulgate but is not part of the Critical Edition's constituted text; it is widely known through popular retellings.
Whatever its textual status, the Durvasa episode is often cited in devotional traditions as an example of Krishna protecting Draupadi, alongside the popular understanding of the disrobing scene.
Jayadratha's Abduction Attempt: Jayadratha, king of Sindhu and husband of Duhshala, the Kauravas' only sister, saw Draupadi alone in the Kamyaka hermitage while the Pandavas were hunting.
Jayadratha's companion Kotikasya questioned Draupadi; Jayadratha then proposed she leave her exiled husbands for him, and when she refused he carried her off in his chariot.
On learning of the abduction, the Pandavas pursued; Draupadi, from Jayadratha's chariot, pointed out each of her husbands to him and described his prowess.
Jayadratha's army was defeated; he fled, but Bhima and Arjuna caught him. Yudhishthira forbade killing him for the sake of Duhshala and Gandhari.
Bhima shaved Jayadratha's head, leaving five tufts of hair, and made him declare himself a slave before releasing him.

Humiliated, Jayadratha did austerities to Shiva and received a boon to hold back all the Pandavas except Arjuna for one day in battle; this boon leads to Abhimanyu's death in the Chakravyuha on the thirteenth day of the war.
Number facts — Jayadratha episode: Tufts of hair left on his head 5 | Pandavas he could hold back with Shiva's boon 4 (all but Arjuna) | Days the boon could apply 1.
Karna's Armour Given to Indra: Karna was born with natural armour (kavacha) and earrings (kundala), which made him almost invulnerable, according to the epic.
Indra, Arjuna's father, planned to beg them from Karna while disguised as a brahmin, knowing Karna never refused a brahmin's request at his midday worship.
The sun god Surya, Karna's father, warned Karna in a dream and urged him not to give the armour away; Karna replied that he would not abandon his vow of generosity even at the cost of his life.
Surya advised Karna at least to ask Indra for his unfailing spear (shakti) in exchange.

Karna cut the armour and earrings from his body and gave them to Indra; Indra gave him a spear that could kill any one enemy but only once, after which it would return to Indra, and promised his body would be left unscarred.
The epithet Vaikartana is often explained as 'the cutter' from this act, though the name is also explained as a patronymic connected with the sun (Vikartana).
Karna saved the spear for Arjuna, but used it on the fourteenth night of the war against Ghatotkacha, leaving him defenceless against Arjuna later.
Popular retellings elaborate the kavacha-kundala details, for example claims about their divine origin and powers; the core of the episode is in the Kundala-harana sub-parva of the Vana Parva.
Yaksha Prashna — the Questions at the La: At the end of the twelfth year, a deer carried off a brahmin's fire-drill sticks (arani) on its antlers, and the Pandavas chased it until they were exhausted and thirsty.

Nakula, then Sahadeva, Arjuna and Bhima went to a lake for water; a voice, from a yaksha in the form of a crane, told each to answer its questions before drinking. Each drank without answering and fell dead.
Yudhishthira came last, agreed to answer, and was asked a long series of riddling questions on nature, life, duty and the self.

Examples of the questions in paraphrase: what is heavier than the earth (the mother); what is higher than the sky (the father); what is swifter than the wind (the mind); what is more numerous than grass (thoughts).
Asked what the greatest wonder is, Yudhishthira answered, in paraphrase, that every day creatures die, yet the living behave as though they will live forever.
Asked what the path is, Yudhishthira said that reasoning is unsettled and scriptures differ, so the path is the one the great have walked.
Offered the life of one brother, Yudhishthira chose Nakula, so that Madri as well as Kunti would have a living son; pleased with this impartiality, the yaksha revived all four.
The yaksha revealed himself as Dharma (identified with Yama), Yudhishthira's father, who had also been the deer; he returned the fire-sticks.
Dharma's boons: that the Pandavas would not be recognised during the thirteenth year, even in their own forms, and that Yudhishthira's mind would remain set on dharma.
The number of questions differs between manuscripts and editions, so no single count should be treated as authoritative; the episode is told in the Araneya sub-parva near the end of the Vana Parva.
Sources for the Exile: The forest exile is told in the Vana Parva (also called Aranyaka Parva, Book 3), one of the longest books of the epic (second in length only to the Shanti Parva); the Critical Edition's Aranyaka Parva has 299 chapters (adhyayas).

Sub-parvas of the Vana Parva include Aranyaka, Kirmira-vadha, Kairata, Indralokabhigamana, Nalopakhyana, Tirthayatra, Jatasura-vadha, Yaksha-yuddha, Nivatakavacha-yuddha, Ajagara, Markandeya-samasya, Draupadi-Satyabhama-samvada, Ghosha-yatra, Mrigasvapnodbhava, Vrihidraunika, Draupadi-harana, Jayadratha-vimokshana, Ramopakhyana, Pativrata-mahatmya, Kundala-harana and Araneya.
Number facts — Critical Edition adhyaya counts: Aranyaka (Vana) Parva 299 | Virata Parva 67.
Much of the Vana Parva consists of stories told to the exiles (Nala, Rama, Savitri, many tirtha legends), which frame the Pandavas' suffering within older tales of loss and restoration.

Preparing for the Incognito Year: For the thirteenth year the Pandavas chose the kingdom of the Matsyas, ruled by King Virata from his city (also called Virata), as their hiding place.
Dhaumya advised them on how to live safely in a king's service: be discreet, do not seek the king's seat or favourites, speak only when asked, and never reveal secrets.

They hid their weapons, including the Gandiva bow, bound up in a shami tree near a cremation ground outside the city; the text says they also hung a corpse in the tree and told passing herdsmen it was the body of their aged mother, hung there by family custom, so that people would keep away.
Among themselves they used secret code names: Yudhishthira was Jaya, Bhima Jayanta, Arjuna Vijaya, Nakula Jayatsena and Sahadeva Jayadbala.
Dhaumya went to Panchala, and their charioteers and servants were sent away to Dvaraka or Panchala with instructions to say they did not know where the Pandavas were.
Code names table: Yudhishthira Jaya | Bhima Jayanta | Arjuna Vijaya | Nakula Jayatsena | Sahadeva Jayadbala.
Disguises of the Pandavas and Draupadi: Yudhishthira became Kanka, a brahmin courtier and dice-playing companion of King Virata, claiming to have been a friend of Yudhishthira.
Bhima became Ballava (Vallabha), a cook in the royal kitchens who also wrestled, claiming to have been Yudhishthira's cook.
Arjuna became Brihannala, a eunuch (under Urvashi's curse) who taught dance and music to Princess Uttara and the palace women, wearing women's dress, bangles and braided hair.
Nakula became Granthika, keeper and trainer of King Virata's horses; some versions name him Damagranthi.
Sahadeva became Tantipala, keeper of King Virata's cattle; some versions name him Arishtanemi.

Draupadi became Sairandhri, a chambermaid and hairdresser to Queen Sudeshna, calling herself Malini and claiming to have served Draupadi and Satyabhama; she said five gandharva husbands secretly protected her.

Disguises table (Pandava = disguise name, role): Yudhishthira = Kanka, brahmin dice companion to the king | Bhima = Ballava, royal cook and wrestler | Arjuna = Brihannala, eunuch dance teacher | Nakula = Granthika, horse-keeper | Sahadeva = Tantipala, cattle-keeper | Draupadi = Sairandhri (Malini), queen's maid.

Each disguise reverses status: the emperor serves as courtier, the warrior as cook, the greatest archer as a dance teacher in women's dress, princes as stable and cattle hands, and the empress as a maid.
Life at Virata's Court: During a festival, Bhima, as Ballava, killed a famous wrestler named Jimuta, winning great praise and rewards from King Virata.
The Pandavas secretly shared their earnings among themselves: Yudhishthira the gains from dice, Bhima food from the kitchen, Arjuna the gifts from the palace women.
Queen Sudeshna hesitated to employ Sairandhri at first, fearing her beauty would attract King Virata.
The text places the Kichaka crisis late in the year, after roughly ten months had passed.
Kichaka: Kichaka, Queen Sudeshna's brother and commander of the Matsya army, was the real military power in Virata, and had repeatedly defeated the neighbouring Trigartas.
Kichaka pursued Sairandhri; when she refused him, he persuaded his sister Sudeshna to send her to his house to fetch wine.
Sairandhri fled into the royal assembly hall; Kichaka followed and kicked her in front of King Virata and Kanka (Yudhishthira), and the king did not punish him.
Yudhishthira, seeing Bhima about to explode, silenced him so as not to break their cover, and told Sairandhri to return to the women's quarters.
That night Draupadi went to Bhima in the kitchen and told him of her humiliation, comparing her life as a maid with her former life as queen.
Bhima told her to arrange a meeting with Kichaka at night in the dance hall (nartanagara); Bhima waited there in the dark, wrestled Kichaka and killed him, crushing his body into a shapeless mass.
Kichaka's brothers, the Upakichakas, blamed Sairandhri and tried to burn her alive on Kichaka's funeral pyre; Bhima, disguised, uprooted a tree and killed all of them.
Number facts — Kichaka episode: Upakichakas (Kichaka's brothers) killed by Bhima 105.
The city believed Sairandhri's gandharva husbands had killed Kichaka, and Sudeshna asked her to leave; she asked to stay just thirteen more days, until the end of the incognito year.
These events form the Kichaka-vadha sub-parva of the Virata Parva.
The Kauravas' Search for the Pandavas: Duryodhana's spies searched everywhere for the Pandavas without success, because finding them before the year ended would send them into exile again.
Bhishma advised that wherever Yudhishthira lived, the land would prosper, with timely rain and contented people.

News that Kichaka had been killed by 'gandharvas' suggested Bhima's strength; Susharma, king of the Trigartas and an old enemy of Kichaka, proposed raiding the Matsya kingdom now that its commander was dead.
The Kauravas agreed to a double raid: the Trigartas would attack first from one direction, and the Kauravas would strike from the other the next day.
The Cattle Raid — Trigarta Attack: Susharma and the Trigartas raided Virata's cattle; Virata led out his army, taking Kanka, Ballava, Granthika and Tantipala with him in chariots, while Arjuna stayed behind as Brihannala.
Susharma captured King Virata in the battle; at Yudhishthira's word, Bhima rescued him and captured Susharma, and Yudhishthira had Susharma released.
Virata, grateful, offered the disguised Pandavas wealth and honours, still not knowing who they were.
The Trigarta attack was planned as a diversion: by drawing King Virata and his army away, it left the capital exposed to the Kaurava raid from the other side the next day.
The Cattle Raid — Kaurava Attack and Bri: While Virata was away, Duryodhana, Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, Karna, Ashwatthama and the Kaurava army raided the Matsya herds from the other side.
Prince Uttara (Bhuminjaya), Virata's young son, boasted before the palace women that he would defeat the Kurus if only he had a charioteer; on Sairandhri's advice, Brihannala was sent as charioteer.
When Uttara saw the Kaurava army, he panicked and jumped from the chariot to flee; Brihannala caught him, made him take the reins, and drove to the shami tree.
Uttara brought down the Pandavas' weapons from the shami tree, and Arjuna revealed his identity, explaining his ten names and their meanings to convince the prince.
Arjuna's ten names, as he lists them: Arjuna, Phalguna, Jishnu, Kiritin, Shvetavahana, Bibhatsu, Vijaya, Krishna, Savyasachin and Dhananjaya.
Arjuna blew his conch Devadatta and strung the Gandiva; Drona recognised the sound and signs of Arjuna's coming.
Before the battle, the Kaurava commanders quarrelled: Karna boasted he would defeat Arjuna alone; Kripa and Ashwatthama rebuked him; Bhishma calmed them.

Arjuna first drove off the raiders and turned the captured cattle back toward Virata, then defeated the Kaurava leaders in a series of duels, including Karna, Kripa, Drona, Ashwatthama, Bhishma and Duryodhana.
Arjuna then used the stupefying weapon (sammohana) to make the whole Kaurava force unconscious; Bhishma alone knew how to counter it.

Remembering Princess Uttara's request for cloth for her dolls, Arjuna had the prince take the upper garments of the unconscious leaders, warning him to keep away from Bhishma, who was still conscious; he did not harm the fallen.
Was the Year Complete? The Dispute: Duryodhana claimed that Arjuna had been recognised before the thirteenth year was over, so the Pandavas must go back into exile for another twelve years.
Bhishma reckoned the time and declared that the Pandavas had completed thirteen years, with time to spare, before Arjuna revealed himself.
Bhishma's reasoning was based on the lunar calendar, which adds intercalary months to keep in step with the solar year: two extra months every five years.
By this reckoning, Bhishma said, the Pandavas had completed the thirteen years plus five months and twelve nights by the day of the cattle raid.
Number facts — Bhishma's reckoning: Years completed 13 | Extra months 5 | Extra nights 12 | Intercalary months per five years 2.
Duryodhana refused to accept the reckoning and to return the kingdom, a refusal that set the Udyoga Parva negotiations in motion.
Whether Bhishma's calculation was correct, and whether lunar or solar years should count, has been discussed by commentators; the epic presents Bhishma's verdict as authoritative.
Revelation and the Wedding of Abhimanyu: Returning home after his rescue, King Virata praised his son Uttara for the victory; Kanka said the credit belonged to Brihannala.
Enraged, Virata threw the dice at Kanka's face and made his nose bleed; Sairandhri caught the blood in a vessel so that none fell on the ground.

The reason given: Arjuna had vowed to kill anyone who shed Yudhishthira's blood except in battle, and Yudhishthira's blood falling on the ground would bring ruin; so Brihannala was kept out until the bleeding stopped.
Prince Uttara privately told his father that a godlike youth, not he, had won the battle.
On the third day after the battle, the five Pandavas, dressed royally, took their seats among the kings in Virata's hall and revealed themselves; Virata begged forgiveness.
Virata offered his daughter Uttara to Arjuna as a bride; Arjuna declined, as he had been her teacher and regarded her as a daughter, and accepted her instead as wife for his son Abhimanyu.
The wedding of Abhimanyu and Uttara was held at Upaplavya in the Matsya kingdom, attended by Krishna, Balarama and the Yadavas, Drupada, and allied kings.
Their son Parikshit, born after the war, became the heir of the Kuru line; the alliance with Matsya and Panchala formed the core of the Pandava coalition.
These events form the Go-grahana (cattle seizure) and Vaivahika (wedding) sub-parvas of the Virata Parva.
Sources and Interpretations of the Virat: The incognito year is told in the Virata Parva (Book 4), a relatively short book compared with the Adi and Vana Parvas or the war books; the Critical Edition's Virata Parva has 67 chapters (adhyayas).
Sub-parvas of the Virata Parva: Pandava-pravesha (entry into Virata), Samaya-palana (keeping the agreement), Kichaka-vadha, Go-grahana and Vaivahika.
Many readers note the Virata Parva's comic and theatrical tone, with role reversals, mistaken identity and boasting, compared with the darker books around it.

Arjuna's life as Brihannala has been discussed in modern scholarship and in queer readings of the epic as an example of gender fluidity in the tradition; the epic itself presents it as the result of Urvashi's curse used as a disguise.
Regional traditions, especially in South India and in Draupadi worship cults, retell the Kichaka episode with extra details; these should be distinguished from the Sanskrit epic.
